item.title: Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Cloudflare has announced a new feature that makes it easier for AI agents to find and retrieve relevant information from

The post Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Cloudflare has announced a new feature that makes it easier for AI agents to find and retrieve relevant information from websites, helping site owners make their content directly searchable by agents at the flick of a switch.

However, doing so could come at a cost to website owners, who are responsible for the associated search infrastructure charges.

Search for Agents, as it’s called, builds on other initiatives from Cloudflare designed to make the web more accessible to AI systems. Last month, the company officially launched AI Search, a managed service that enables developers to index their own data and integrate search functionality into applications and agents. And this serves as the underlying search infrastructure for Search for Agents.

Back in February, Cloudflare also launched Markdown for Agents, which automatically converts HTML pages into a lightweight, text-based format that AI agents can consume more efficiently — part of a broader evolution of the web to accommodate both human and machine visitors.

Search for Agents takes this further by giving websites their own agent-discoverable search API, allowing agents to query a site’s content directly without having to navigate individual pages to find the information they need.

The agent retrieval problem

Back in September, developer documentation platform Mintlify highlighted a problem with llms.txt, a file that serves AI agents with a map of a website’s content. Larger documentation sites were hitting Mintlify’s 100,000-character limit for these files, resulting in some pages being omitted. The company addressed this by introducing a hierarchy of smaller index files, allowing agents to discover all available pages without having to load the entire index.

The issue was particularly pertinent for Mintlify, which reported in April that AI coding agents accounted for 45.3% of requests across documentation sites powered by its platform, almost on a par with traditional browser traffic.

Cloudflare, for its part, also reported last year that AI crawling triggered by users’ queries had increased more than twentyfold through 2025.

Even with improvements such as those introduced by Mintlify, agents still have to navigate a website’s content index to find the information they need. Search for Agents seeks to bypass that process by allowing agents to query the website directly.

In a blog post published on Wednesday, the company detailed how website operators can enable the feature, currently in beta, via the Quick Actions section of their domain’s Cloudflare dashboard or programmatically through an API.

Once activated, Cloudflare provisions a dedicated AI Search instance and begins crawling and indexing the website’s content. Website operators can subsequently manage that instance from their AI Search dashboard, adjusting settings such as caching and enabling reranking to improve the relevance of search results.

Cloudflare also inserts instructions into the metadata of each page, telling visiting agents where the search API resides and how to use it. For websites that have enabled Markdown for Agents, these instructions are also included in the Markdown document’s YAML front matter.

Agents can then send keywords or natural-language questions to the website’s /.well-known/search endpoint, receiving relevant excerpts from the site’s content in Markdown. The agent can use this to formulate its own response to the user’s question.

Who pays for agent search?

Search for Agents is available across all Cloudflare plans, including its free tier. However, with AI Search billing set to begin on December 1, there are cost considerations for website owners looking to make their content more accessible to AI agents.

Each account receives a monthly allowance of 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-months of storage, and 1,000 queries each for semantic and full-text search. Beyond those allowances, Cloudflare charges $0.75 per million ingestion tokens, $2 per GB-month of storage, $0.75 per 1,000 semantic, vector or hybrid queries, and $0.10 per 1,000 full-text queries.

Moreover, there are limits on how much content Cloudflare can crawl to populate the search index. Customers on the Workers Free plan are limited to 500 pages per day, while paying customers face no daily crawl limit. Both are subject to a 100,000-page limit per discovery crawl.

This raises an interesting question in the context of Cloudflare’s broader efforts to help website owners monetize AI traffic. Last July, the company introduced pay-per-crawl, enabling website owners to charge AI companies for fetching individual pages. The company expanded on that initiative this July with a push toward pay-per-use, whereby publishers would be compensated when their content appears in AI-generated answers. It’s part of a broader effort, as The New Stack reported at the time, to build the economic layer of the AI web.

Then in September, Cloudflare launched its Monetization Gateway in closed beta, enabling domain owners to charge AI agents for accessing websites, APIs, MCP tools and datasets using the x402 payment protocol.

Against that backdrop, the economics of Search for Agents are particularly striking. Having spent much of the past 18 months developing ways for website owners to generate revenue from AI traffic, Cloudflare is now asking those same website owners to shoulder the cost of making their content more readily accessible to AI agents.

“Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner.”

So what incentive do website owners have to absorb these costs? According to Celso Martinho, VP of engineering at Cloudflare, it comes down to the growing importance of AI agents as an audience in their own right.

“Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner,” Martinho tells The New Stack.

For context, Cloudflare reported back in June that bots, which include AI agents, accounted for 57% of HTML page requests across its network. Martinho also points to existing tools such as Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control and the x402 payment protocol, which website operators can use to manage and monetize access to their content.

Moreover, plans are afoot to extend Cloudflare’s Monetization Gateway to cover the new search endpoints, which would enable website owners to charge agents directly for search queries.

“We are working on adding first-class support for Search for Agents and other agentic content APIs to Monetization Gateway,” Martinho says, though no timeline was provided.

For now, those search costs fall to website owners.

A common language for agent search?

While companies can, of course, build and expose their own search APIs, Search for Agents essentially gives Cloudflare customers an off-the-shelf solution. According to Martinho, existing agents with web browsing capabilities should be able to discover and use these endpoints without developers having to build dedicated integrations.

Cloudflare has tested the approach extensively across its own blog and developer documentation sites, Martinho says, “demonstrating that using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”

“Using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”

There have been broader efforts across the industry to standardize how AI agents interact with the world around them. Last December, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), of which Cloudflare is a founding member, bringing projects such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), AGENTS.md and Goose under a common umbrella.

For now, though, Cloudflare is pursuing its own approach to search endpoint discovery.

“Agents do a pretty good job at adjusting to different instructions and web protocols,” Martinho says, adding that Cloudflare’s research into agent behavior through initiatives such as Radar’s AI Insights and its Agent Readiness project informed its choice of technologies for Search for Agents.

Cloudflare’s approach draws on established web conventions such as well-known URIs and HTTP GET, alongside the newer HTTP QUERY method, an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) proposed standard co-authored by Cloudflare engineer James Snell.

However, Martinho acknowledges the merits of a broader industry effort in this area.

“Interoperability absolutely matters,” Martinho says. “A common approach to discovering search endpoints across providers would also make sense.”

The post Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill. appeared first on The New Stack.
Cloudflare already helps sites charge AI companies for content. But its new search feature puts site owners on the hook for agent queries beyond a free monthly allowance.

item.title: AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works?
item.dc:creator: Mayank Ahluwalia
item.description:
As organizations invest in AI, many are discovering a new bottleneck: obtaining data that is both protected and useful. Engineering

The post AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
As organizations invest in AI, many are discovering a new bottleneck: obtaining data that is both protected and useful. Engineering teams need realistic, production-like data to validate AI-generated changes, train models, test applications, and generate business insights.

Yet, privacy initiatives can sometimes make that data harder to access, less representative of real-world conditions, or unable to preserve critical relationships between records. 

The Perforce Delphix “2026 State of AI and Data Privacy Report” highlights this challenge. Among surveyed organizations, 26% say privacy controls make production-quality data harder to obtain, 25% struggle to preserve relationships across data entities, and 51% cite data quality challenges. 

“Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it.”

Protecting data isn’t enough if it can no longer support the systems that depend on it. For engineering teams, the question is whether their data protection strategies can preserve the qualities that make data valuable in the first place. You need a well-rounded data strategy with tools that maintain referential integrity and relationships across your environments.

What these statistics mean for practitioners

At first glance, statistics from the report, like “51% of enterprises cite data quality challenges,” may sound like a purely governance issue.

In practice, they represent engineering problems. Low-quality datasets can produce:

  • Inaccurate analytics.
  • Poorly trained AI models.
  • Incomplete test coverage.
  • Increased rework.
  • Delayed releases.
  • Reduced confidence in data automation.

“When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable.”

When an AI model is trained on incomplete or distorted data, its outputs become less reliable. When test environments contain unrealistic data, defects can escape into production. When analytics datasets lack consistency, teams spend more time validating results than acting on them.

Data protection and utility are not opposing goals

A common misconception is that organizations must choose between privacy and innovation, but the most successful organizations know that compliance, quality, and speed can and need to work together.

Protected data still needs to be:

  • Realistic enough for testing and validation.
  • Representative enough for analytics.
  • Accessible enough for engineering teams.
  • Governed enough for regulatory requirements.
  • Connected enough to preserve referential integrity.

There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection. All too often, enterprises sacrifice compliance for innovation or speed. That’s a big reason 84% of respondents in our report have a data privacy exception in their non-production environments.

“There’s a two-fold goal in the AI era: reduce sensitive data exposure while also creating trusted data that remains valuable after protection.”

Organizations can only move at AI speed when they have access to trustworthy data that accurately represents production conditions. When privacy controls degrade quality, limit realism, or restrict access to representative datasets, the data layer becomes the new bottleneck.

Why referential integrity matters more than ever

Many discussions about data privacy focus on masking sensitive fields. However, masked data that loses referential integrity between entities can create a different kind of risk.

A customer, order, or payment record may still exist, but if the relationships connecting those records break during protection processes, the data no longer resembles reality. Take billing validation, for example. It needs referential integrity when a customer has multiple products, charges, and invoices across several database tables to produce the correct products or make accurate charges. 

Broken relationships are especially problematic for modern AI and analytics systems. Analytics pipelines depend on consistent identifiers to join information across sources. AI and machine learning workflows depend on complete business context to identify patterns and make predictions. Software testing depends on realistic relationships between records to validate application behavior accurately.

When referential integrity is lost:

  • Analytics can produce incomplete or misleading results.
  • AI models can learn from flawed datasets.
  • Testing environments can fail to expose production issues.
  • Teams lose trust in protected datasets.

Importantly, these failures are often difficult to detect. Pipelines may continue running successfully while quietly producing degraded outcomes, which can be a very costly mistake.

This helps explain why 25% of surveyed organizations cited preserving relationships across data entities as a significant challenge. For practitioners, that statistic is a warning that privacy controls can unintentionally undermine the quality of AI and analytics initiatives if they fail to preserve business context.

Keep in mind that not all data protection solutions are created equal — enterprise-grade masking algorithms are key to preserving relationships. When applied consistently and at scale, these algorithms ensure the same input produces the same masked output across your systems and environments. Other masking approaches might be done piecemeal, resulting in broken relationships.

What engineering teams should measure

Many organizations measure privacy success through compliance metrics alone. However, AI-driven environments require a broader definition of success. Engineering leaders should evaluate privacy initiatives against several dimensions:

  • Data quality: Does the protected dataset accurately reflect production conditions?
  • Realism: Can developers, data scientists, and analysts use the data confidently for their intended purpose?
  • Referential integrity: Do relationships remain consistent across applications, tables, environments, and data sources?
  • Accessibility: Can teams obtain compliant data without introducing delays?
  • Provisioning speed: How quickly can trusted datasets be delivered when needed?

These measurements help organizations determine whether privacy efforts enable AI outcomes or create new obstacles.

Designing for governance by default

As AI adoption grows, privacy cannot remain a separate process that occurs after development begins. Organizations should instead map the entire data lifecycle, from data request and discovery to reuse and retirement. 

This approach helps ensure governance is built into workflows rather than applied as a late-stage checkpoint. It also provides stronger auditability, reduces compliance exceptions, and gives teams greater confidence that protected datasets remain fit for purpose.

Most importantly, it aligns privacy objectives with business outcomes instead of treating them as competing priorities.

Trusted data will become a competitive differentiator

The need for test data — in volume, coverage, and scale — is booming as agentic development continues to rise. AI has also increased the volume of change enterprises can generate, but the challenge of validating that change remains unsolved.

That responsibility still belongs to data. The organizations that gain the most value from AI will not necessarily be the ones with the most advanced models. They will be the ones with the most trustworthy data foundations — using a portfolio approach that combines data virtualization for speed, masking for security, and synthetic data for coverage as needed.

“In the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.”

The research points to a clear lesson: If privacy controls uphold realism, quality, relationships between records, or access to representative datasets, they can enable AI success.

As enterprises continue investing in AI and data privacy, the real objective should be ensuring protection and utility coexist. Because in the AI era, trusted data, not fast model output, may be the ultimate competitive advantage.

The post AI wrote the code. Can your test data tell you if it works? appeared first on The New Stack.
Learn how to protect enterprise data without sacrificing AI model reliability, referential integrity, or engineering velocity.

item.title: A developer ran 50 agents at once. Then his Mac became the bottleneck.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:

The post A developer ran 50 agents at once. Then his Mac became the bottleneck. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
As developers move from working with individual AI coding agents to orchestrating dozens of concurrent sessions, the hardware they use to develop software is becoming a potential bottleneck.

In a post on X Monday, a developer named Pranit described how running more than 50 concurrent agent sessions exposed the biggest bottleneck in his development workflow: his Mac.

Vercel CTO Malte Ubl responded that he had encountered the same limitations in his own development workflow.

“No single computer is fast enough to keep up with dozens of agents working on parallel.”

“No single computer is fast enough to keep up with dozens of agents working on parallel,” Ubl writes.

Rather than moving the agents themselves to the cloud, Ubl keeps them running locally and offloads builds and tests to remote sandboxes. Developers can retain their existing tools and workflows without being constrained by the compute capacity of a single machine.

“Dozens of agents can all decide to run a build at the same time,” Ubl tells The New Stack. “They’re competing for the same machine, and everything slows down.”

When agents outrun one machine

Even when model inference runs in the cloud, compilation, dependency management, and test execution initiated by coding agents can place significant demands on local CPU and memory.

Separating agent orchestration from code execution lets developers scale those workloads independently of their local hardware.

Separating orchestration from execution

Developers can install the Vercel Plugin by running npx plugins add vercel/vercel-plugin and then instruct their coding agents to offload builds and tests to remote sandboxes.

One technical challenge of remote execution is maintaining consistency between the local workspace and the sandbox, particularly when agents modify code that hasn’t been committed.

Ubl tells The New Stack that execution begins from a snapshot with dependencies already installed. The current source code, including uncommitted edits and new files that aren’t excluded by Git ignore rules, is then copied to the sandbox. Dependencies persist in the remote environment and are updated when they change.

“You shouldn’t have to commit and push just to test what an agent is working on.”

“You shouldn’t have to commit and push just to test what an agent is working on,” Ubl says.

Unlike conventional CI workflows triggered by repository events, this approach brings remote execution into the development feedback loop itself.

Agents can validate changes before committing, and computationally expensive tasks no longer need to compete for the same local resources.

When remote execution pays off

There is no specific number of concurrent agents at which remote execution becomes more efficient than running builds and tests locally.

The crossover depends on the project’s computational requirements, the frequency of builds and tests, network latency, and the cost of provisioning remote infrastructure.

“You have to weigh the upload, setup time and cloud compute cost against the time saved.”

“You have to weigh the upload, setup time and cloud compute cost against the time saved,” Ubl tells The New Stack. “Warm snapshots help.”

In Seoul, regional image caching brought sandbox startup times down from roughly 3.5 seconds to 1.05 seconds, according to benchmarks published by Vercel.

But spinning up a sandbox is only part of the equation. Developers still have to transfer source files and pay for remote compute. Vercel did not provide benchmarks comparing the total time or cost of running builds and tests locally versus remotely.

Local execution may still make more sense when running a handful of agents on a small codebase. The economics could change when dozens of agents compete for CPU and memory to run builds and tests concurrently.

Local development goes distributed

Remote build systems and cloud-based development environments predate AI coding agents. What’s changing is the number of concurrent workloads an individual engineer can generate.

“As developers run more agents in parallel, I expect this split to become common,” Ubl tells The New Stack.

The post A developer ran 50 agents at once. Then his Mac became the bottleneck. appeared first on The New Stack.
Running dozens of AI coding agents at once can max out your Mac. Vercel’s fix keeps agents local and offloads builds and tests to remote sandboxes.

item.title: Cognition’s new engineers aren’t even downloading code anymore — they build entirely through Devin
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Some engineers joining Cognition no longer set up local development environments. Instead, Devin has become their primary interface for software

The post Cognition’s new engineers aren’t even downloading code anymore — they build entirely through Devin appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Some engineers joining Cognition no longer set up local development environments. Instead, Devin has become their primary interface for software development.

Speaking to Patrick O’Shaughnessy on Tuesday’s episode of Invest Like the Best, Cognition co-founder and CEO Scott Wu describes how the company’s internal engineering practices have changed as coding agents have become more capable.

No terminal, no download

“The funniest moment for me, I would say, was actually around like four or five months ago when we started to realize that new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer,” Wu says. “Like they didn’t pull up a terminal. They didn’t run a command line or anything.”

“new engineers that joined our team just didn’t even download the code on their computer … They didn’t run a command line or anything.”

Over roughly a year, Cognition doubled its engineering headcount while increasing its rate of merged pull requests 20-fold, Wu says. That amounts to approximately ten times as many merged pull requests per engineer, despite the company’s already extensive use of AI coding tools a year earlier.

Perhaps more significant, Wu estimates, is that approximately 90% of Cognition’s internal Devin usage is now automated in some form.

When Devin runs itself

Wu cites incident response as an example of Cognition’s automated Devin workflows, where an error can trigger an investigation before an on-call engineer intervenes.

“It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off.”

“It doesn’t involve a human saying, ‘Hey, Devin, I need you to go work on this thing’ to kick it off,” Wu says.

Although Wu does not specify whether the 90% figure represents session count, token consumption, or another metric, automated execution has implications for compute provisioning and budget allocation as inference demand becomes less dependent on individual developer activity.

Cognition has already introduced hierarchical budgets for Devin, which give enterprises spending controls across organizational levels.

250,000 pull requests monthly

Wu says one of Cognition’s largest banking customers was on track to merge 250,000 pull requests with Devin in October. Until a few months earlier, the entire organization had been merging approximately 400,000 pull requests per month.

The bank has approximately 80,000 engineering personnel, according to Wu, and only a fraction of the organization had been fully onboarded to Devin at the time of the interview.

Separately, Citi CEO Jane Fraser says during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call that 14,000 engineers use Devin.

Neither Cognition’s internal figures nor the banking customer’s projected PR volume account for the complexity of individual changes. Wu does not provide corresponding data on change failure rates or review workloads, metrics that would help establish whether the rest of the SDLC has kept pace with implementation.

The disparity between implementation and review capacity has already prompted vendors such as CodeRabbit to expand into agentic change management.

Wu argues that enterprise adoption also requires engineering leaders to reconsider their roadmaps and organizational structures to accommodate additional implementation capacity.

Watching the agent swarms

The shift from individual background agents to swarms is a particular concern for Wu because monitoring becomes more difficult when multiple agents work together.

Cognition has been exploring this execution model with its recently introduced Devin Bots, persistent agents that manage other agents’ work.

Wu stresses the need to catch unintended agent behavior early and limit what agents can access, especially when workflows run without an engineer supervising them.

The engineering skill ceiling hasn’t changed

“The barrier to entry has for sure gotten a lot lower,” Wu says. “However, I think the skill ceiling and, you know, a lot of the particular skill sets that you need are still very much the same as they always have been.”

“I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable.”

For Wu, writing code is only one part of software engineering. Engineers still have to figure out what an incomplete or ambiguous specification actually means and make architectural decisions that could affect the business for years, even if an agent handles the implementation.

“I think people who can do that really well have always been valuable and now they’re just 10 times more valuable,” Wu says.

New engineers at Cognition don’t download the code anymore — CEO Scott Wu says roughly 90% of internal Devin usage now runs without a human trigger.

item.title: Anthropic set more than 1,700 traps for Claude — what it found is both reassuring and unsettling
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:

The post Anthropic set more than 1,700 traps for Claude — what it found is both reassuring and unsettling appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
As coding agents take on longer-running engineering tasks, Anthropic is examining how models behave when their execution environments fail to enforce intended security boundaries.

…documenting a sandbox’s intended isolation properties in the system prompt reduced the likelihood of agents reaching outside their authorized environments by 68% to 96%…

The company’s safeguards team found that explicitly documenting a sandbox’s intended isolation properties in the system prompt reduced the likelihood of agents reaching outside their authorized environments by 68% to 96% across six Claude models.

In research published Tuesday, Anthropic introduced Siren, an internal evaluation designed to measure a model’s propensity to exploit weaknesses in its execution environment to complete otherwise legitimate tasks.

The researchers tested more than 1,700 scenarios across 26 sandbox configurations, including Docker, gVisor and QEMU. Drawing on publicly reported sandbox escapes, they focused primarily on misconfigurations and deliberately placed resources outside the sandbox that could help agents complete routine DevOps assignments.

Reaching outside the sandbox

Anthropic evaluated the six models without the safeguards included in its commercial deployments. The Claude 5.5 series and Claude Mythos 5.2 attempted to access or accessed external resources in 21% to 32% of scenarios.

However, use of those resources that could not reasonably be interpreted as authorized occurred in just 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios, compared with 12.7% for Claude Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Claude Mythos 5.

Anthropic cautioned against interpreting these figures as real-world incident rates.

Spelling out the sandbox rules

Anthropic found that recent models frequently rationalized their use of external resources as permissible within the context of their assignments. Tasks that were impossible to complete within the sandbox produced particularly high rates of boundary-crossing behavior.

Tasks that were impossible to complete within the sandbox produced particularly high rates of boundary-crossing behavior.

Across 366 scenarios involving impossible tasks, removing language that encouraged exhaustive searches and granted broad authority over the machine reduced the frequency of reaching outside the sandbox by 23 to 26 percentage points in five of the six models tested. A separate study earlier this fall found that removing a single sentence pushed Claude Code’s out-of-scope rate from zero to 17.1%.

When researchers spelled out the sandbox’s rules, the rate of reaching outside dropped to around 2% or less for the Claude 5.5 series and Claude Mythos 5.2. Anthropic already uses this approach in Claude Code when sandboxing is enabled.

Reporting weaknesses instead of exploiting

The researchers also gave agents a sanctioned way to report sandbox weaknesses to infrastructure operators and to check whether another agent had already flagged the same problem.

Combined with Anthropic’s auto mode, which uses a classifier to assess whether tool calls align with user intent, the mitigations eliminated measured misaligned use in five of the six models. Claude Mythos 5 recorded a rate of 0.1%.

Two models saw completion rates fall by roughly nine percentage points on tasks achievable within the sandbox, and Anthropic tuned its classifier on the same scenarios used to evaluate it.

When Claude senses the test

Although none of the six models were trained on Siren’s scenarios or transcripts, evaluation awareness ranged from 43% to 67% among the four newest models, compared with 29% and 36% for their predecessors, with Claude Sonnet 5.5 recording the highest rate.

evaluation awareness ranged from 43% to 67% among the four newest models… with Claude Sonnet 5.5 recording the highest rate.

Newer models were also less likely to reach outside their sandboxes, though Anthropic could not establish whether evaluation awareness contributed to that restraint or whether both behaviors resulted from changes in model training.

item.title: OpenAI claims to have solved a 57-year-old math problem at the heart of AI computation
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI claims to have solved a problem that has occupied theoretical computer scientists since 1969. In a preprint published Tuesday

The post OpenAI claims to have solved a 57-year-old math problem at the heart of AI computation appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI claims to have solved a problem that has occupied theoretical computer scientists since 1969. In a preprint published Tuesday on GitHub, the company presents a lower bound for the exponent of square matrix multiplication that matches the upper bound of 2.25 it reported in October.

OpenAI claims to have solved a problem that has occupied theoretical computer scientists since 1969.

If the proof holds, developers working on numerical libraries and AI infrastructure will know where the mathematical limit lies and can focus on other ways to improve performance.

The paper is one of nine manuscripts OpenAI released Tuesday, seven of which apply a new geometric theory of tensors to problems in arithmetic complexity and combinatorics.

Bounding the exponent at 2.25

In 1969, Volker Strassen showed that two n × n matrices could be multiplied with an arithmetic exponent below three, prompting researchers to see how close they could get to two.

The previous record was approximately 2.371 before OpenAI claimed an upper bound of 2.25 over the complex numbers in an October 2 preprint.

Independent researchers weigh in

Researchers Mahmut Levent Doğan, Vladimir Lysikov, Keiya Sakabe, and Michael Walter from LMU Munich in Germany published their own exposition of the proof earlier this month.

The researchers arrived at the same upper bound over arbitrary fields by substituting a variant of the tensor value introduced by IBM researchers Don Coppersmith and Shmuel Winograd for the spectral points used in OpenAI’s original proof.

OpenAI approaches the problem through a computational lower bound for determining whether the entries in several independent lists are distinct.

In Tuesday’s 111-page manuscript, “The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths,” OpenAI approaches the problem through a computational lower bound for determining whether the entries in several independent lists are distinct.

In a companion paper on tensor geometry, OpenAI develops the mathematical framework for its argument that bringing the exponent below 2.25 would allow certain tensor networks to be compressed in violation of the lower bound for the distinctness problem.

The authors put the lower bound for multiplying two n × n matrices at ⌈n²·²⁵/2⌉ nonscalar multiplications or divisions in a formal arithmetic circuit, even if linear operations are free and for any n ≥ 2.

What Lean actually verifies

OpenAI released a Lean formalization alongside the manuscript as developers explore AI-assisted formal verification in software engineering.

The LMU Munich researchers also published their own Lean formalization of the upper-bound proof in November. Their implementation establishes the bound in terms of asymptotic tensor rank but does not formalize the arithmetic computational model discussed in their paper.

One limitation noted in OpenAI’s documentation is that the Lean proofs cover formal polynomial identities over arbitrary fields using division-free arithmetic programs. The lower bound for circuits that permit division has not been formalized in Lean as part of this release.

In OpenAI’s Lean source code, the square exponent theorem relies on two imported theorems that connect the formal arithmetic model to the matrix multiplication exponent.

OpenAI presents an exact formula for rectangular matrix multiplication exponents and puts the dual exponent at 0.5, which would mean that multiplying an n × n matrix by an n × ⌈nᵗ⌉ matrix has an arithmetic exponent of two for values of t between zero and 0.5.

On October 7, OpenAI withdrew three manuscripts and revised 14 others. The withdrawals followed the discovery of a sign error in a paper on algebraic geometry that invalidated a construction used in two dependent papers. None of the three concerned matrix multiplication.

GPU performance in practice

The rectangular matrix multiplication results are worth a closer look considering how much activation matrix dimensions vary with batch size and token count in transformer workloads.

Given the different computational demands of prefill and autoregressive decoding, the rectangular exponent may be a more useful result for inference optimization than the square exponent of 2.25.

Given the different computational demands of prefill and autoregressive decoding, the rectangular exponent may be a more useful result for inference optimization than the square exponent of 2.25.

GPU utilization also depends on implementation. Nvidia’s GEMM performance documentation explains how larger tiles can improve data reuse while leaving fewer thread blocks available to keep the GPU busy.

Any claims about lower training or inference costs will have to wait until researchers can benchmark new algorithms against existing CUDA implementations at production matrix sizes and precisions.

OpenAI’s new preprint claims the exponent of square matrix multiplication is exactly 2.25 — what the proof could mean for AI infrastructure developers.

item.title: JetBrains’ latest Mellum coding model uses 45% fewer tokens. It got there by not thinking.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
JetBrains has launched a new variant of its open source coding model, one designed to tackle quick code edits, tool

The post JetBrains’ latest Mellum coding model uses 45% fewer tokens. It got there by not thinking. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
JetBrains has launched a new variant of its open source coding model, one designed to tackle quick code edits, tool calls and all the smaller tasks that AI coding agents perform in the course of solving bigger problems.

Mellum2.1 Instruct, as it’s called, is the latest installment in JetBrains’ in-house coding model lineup. The original Mellum, which debuted back in 2024, was a proprietary model built specifically for low-latency code completion in JetBrains’ IDEs.

Then in June this year, JetBrains introduced Mellum2, a more versatile, 12-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model released under an Apache 2.0 license in both reasoning (Thinking) and non-reasoning (Instruct) variants. While Mellum2 was trained to handle individual coding tasks and tool calls, the next iteration would focus more specifically on how agents operate across entire code repositories.

That came last month with Mellum2.1 Thinking, which retained the same underlying architecture as Mellum2, but with an additional stage of reinforcement learning (RL) in which the model learned to navigate repositories, use shell and file tools, and make changes that would pass hidden tests.

With Mellum2.1 Instruct, JetBrains is now extending that same repository-level training to its non-reasoning model, which generates answers without an explicit chain-of-thought. As with its Thinking sibling, the company used Nvidia’s open source NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge libraries to train the model using infrastructure capable of running 10,000 sandboxes concurrently.

The result is a leaner coding model fine-tuned for speed and token efficiency, capable of handling many of the same agentic tasks as its Thinking counterpart, with about half the token consumption, according to JetBrains’ testing.

The cost of overthinking

In a blog post published on Wednesday, Gleb Ingman, who works on the Mellum model team at JetBrains, notes that Mellum2.1 Instruct was built specifically for “sub-agents, tool loops, and chat.”

In real terms, this means that while Mellum2.1 Thinking is better suited to investigative tasks such as diagnosing why a unit test is failing, much of a coding agent’s day-to-day work involves more straightforward operations, such as modifying a few lines of code or retrieving information from a codebase. It’s these kinds of tasks that Mellum2.1 Instruct is geared toward, either operating independently or handling assignments delegated to it by a more powerful model.

“Every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting.”

“In these cases, reasoning adds time and computing resources without adding quality,” Ingman writes. “This is especially true when the model runs locally — every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting.”

Indeed, in the wake of the Thinking release, Ingman says that JetBrains fielded numerous requests from developers running models locally for a less verbose alternative capable of handling “moderately hard tasks.”

In its own benchmarking, JetBrains pits Mellum2.1 Instruct against the previous Mellum2 Instruct model, as well as Alibaba’s Qwen3.5 9B and Google’s Gemma 4 E4B, with reasoning disabled in both competing models. The six benchmarks cover agentic coding, multilingual code generation, tool use, instruction following and mathematical problem-solving.

Mellum2.1 Instruct doubled its predecessor’s score on SWE-bench Verified, which measures a model’s ability to resolve real-world software issues, jumping from 20.2% to 40.4%. It also outperformed all three models on the MultiPL-E code generation benchmark and broadly matched Qwen3.5 9B on ToolHop, which evaluates multi-step tool use.

Qwen3.5 9B, it’s worth noting, still came out ahead on SWE-bench Verified, scoring 49.8%. However, JetBrains points to Mellum’s MoE architecture, which activates just 2.5 billion of its 12 billion parameters for each token. According to the company’s earlier testing, this enables Mellum2.1 to generate tokens around 1.4 times as fast as Qwen3.5 9B for individual requests and 1.8 times as fast under load.

Perhaps more pertinent to this particular release, though, is how Mellum2.1 Instruct compares with its Thinking sibling in terms of token generation. In JetBrains’ agentic coding tests, the new model generated an average of 5,600 tokens per task, compared with 10,100 for Thinking — a reduction of 45%.

When tokens associated with tool calls were excluded, that reduction rose to 73%.

There are trade-offs, of course. While the two variants perform almost equally well on SWE-bench Verified, the gap widens on benchmarks that draw on competitive programming and mathematics competitions.

“On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice,” Ingman writes.

“On hard algorithmic and math problems…. thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice.”

Mellum2.1 Instruct is available on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license, including a GGUF version for running the model locally on hardware with limited memory. JetBrains is also releasing a multi-token prediction (MTP) head alongside the model, which predicts multiple tokens ahead to accelerate generation by up to 1.8 times, according to the company.

A model for the multi-agent era

Mellum2.1 Instruct arrives as JetBrains increasingly focuses its core developer tools on agent orchestration. In September, the company introduced a revamped version of Air, its development environment for working with multiple coding agents. JetBrains has also been expanding the capabilities of Junie, the coding agent it launched last year, with a renewed emphasis on local execution.

As developers delegate more work to agents, and those agents in turn delegate tasks to other agents, there is clear scope for using different models according to the complexity of the job at hand.

As developers delegate more work to agents, and those agents in turn delegate tasks to other agents, there is clear scope for using different models according to the complexity of the job at hand. A more token-efficient model such as Mellum2.1 Instruct, therefore, could help keep inference costs and latency in check across such a system.

Whether JetBrains intends to deploy Mellum2.1 Instruct in its own agentic products, such as Air or Junie, remains unclear.

item.title: Please don’t give the robot my SSH keys: How to keep AI out of trouble
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
Say a developer asks an AI agent to find out why a Kubernetes pod keeps crashing. The agent needs logs.

The post Please don’t give the robot my SSH keys: How to keep AI out of trouble appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Say a developer asks an AI agent to find out why a Kubernetes pod keeps crashing. The agent needs logs. Depending on what it finds, it may need to look at another service. The developer has credentials that can get it there, but handing those over would give the agent everything those credentials can reach. By the time the pod is healthy again, someone may have a second incident to investigate.

In a conversation with The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City, Teleport field CTO Boris Kurktchiev uses that debugging scenario to explain delegated identity. The agent starts without access and requests what it needs for the job. The audit trail links the person who requested the work to the actions the agent took. A developer can send the agent to investigate without lending it their keys.

“The agent had access on behalf of Boris,” Kurktchiev said.

One access policy across the stack

Teleport’s core platform is designed to give teams a common way to define access across systems that otherwise have their own controls. For developers, that matters when a single investigation takes them from Kubernetes to a database or when a CI/CD pipeline needs access to infrastructure. Kurktchiev describes applying the same policy model to people, automated workloads and agents, with permissions scoped to resources such as a particular pod or database table.

The appeal becomes clearer when one developer launches several agents at once. Each can generate access requests, and a human who has to approve every routine step will eventually run out of patience. As Kurktchiev and Lardinois discuss, the convenience of turning off the prompts starts to look different when the work touches production. The practical question is which decisions a team can encode in policy and which still need a person’s attention.

What happens inside the sandbox

Teleport announced Beams at KubeCon, and Kurktchiev describes it as an agent runtime that combines sandboxing, identity, access, and observability and auditing. Isolation gives an agent a place to run. Teams still have to consider what credentials are available in that environment and what those credentials can reach.

“So just having a sandbox is not enough.”

“So just having a sandbox is not enough,” Kurktchiev told TNS.

With Beams, Kurktchiev says, an agent starts without access. A team can define which resources it should be able to request, for how long, and what an acceptable execution path looks like.

“The default is always zero,” Kurktchiev said.

That approach lets developers distinguish between the plan an agent proposes and the permissions it actually gets. If execution diverges from the plan, Kurktchiev describes options to alert someone, stop the run, or fork it to explore an alternate path. That last option matters because a detour can turn up something worth pursuing. The token bill, the two men joke, is a separate discussion.

“The default is always zero.”

The interview also looks beyond Teleport. Kurktchiev points to SPIFFE as a foundation for machine identity across systems and considers what agents might need from it as they work across organizational boundaries. He also sees work ahead for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which gives agents a way to connect to tools and data. Connecting an agent to a service opens up a second set of questions about what it can do there and how a team will account for it afterward.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear Kurktchiev and Lardinois discuss what it takes to move an agent from a developer’s sandbox into production, how to keep approvals manageable when agents multiply, and what an audit trail needs to show when an investigation takes an unexpected turn.

The post Please don’t give the robot my SSH keys: How to keep AI out of trouble appeared first on The New Stack.
An AI agent can debug a crashing pod without borrowing your keys. Teleport's Boris Kurktchiev explains why agent access should start at zero.

item.title: Move fast, don’t break 100 apps: Dan Garfield on keeping AI-powered coding on the rails
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
An AI coding agent can give a product manager a working prototype before the next planning meeting. Which is great!

The post Move fast, don’t break 100 apps: Dan Garfield on keeping AI-powered coding on the rails appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An AI coding agent can give a product manager a working prototype before the next planning meeting. Which is great! But someone still has to decide whether any interactions make sense, the new features solve a problem, or — most importantly — whether the team can ship it safely. 

At Octopus Deploy, that’s changing how product managers pitch new features. The company is asking them to bring a prototype in place of a written requirements document and keep refining how the feature works, says Dan Garfield, its VP of Open Source. A developer can then take it the rest of the way to production.

“The ultimate differentiator now seems to be care, attention to detail, and taste.”

“The ultimate differentiator now seems to be care, attention to detail, and taste,” Garfield told The New Stack’s Matt Burns at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City. Their conversation moves from talking about a free tool that catches risky Argo CD configurations to a bigger question facing developers who use AI to write code. For example, what happens when the team can produce changes faster than it can verify and deliver them?

A checkup for Argo CD

Garfield, an Argo CD maintainer, recalls a community member whose instance suddenly deleted 100 applications. They recovered quickly, but figuring out what happened took some digging. Two settings that were fine on their own could, together, let a network error trigger the deletions.

That’s the sort of surprise Octo Doctor, a free, open-source tool announced at ArgoCon, is meant to catch. It scans Argo CD configurations against a deterministic rule set drawn from years of maintenance and customer work. Its report explains what a setting could do and how to address it. Developers can run it from the command line, invoke it as a Claude skill, or add it to CI to catch risky pull-request changes.

“It’s a tool that you can run using AI, but it gives you a deterministic output,” Garfield told TNS.

The guidance leaves room for judgment. A team might have good reasons to keep a flagged configuration. The report lets developers weigh that choice with a clearer picture of what could go wrong. Ideally, they get to have that conversation before 100 applications make it for them.

When the bottleneck moves to delivery

In Garfield’s account, more AI-assisted coding puts pressure on source control and then on CI as teams open and revise more pull requests. Once those changes pass CI, developers still need evidence that the software behaves correctly in an environment that resembles production. Octopus Deploy’s continuous delivery platform works with Argo CD and handles steps such as testing, approvals, and promotion from staging to production.

Garfield describes how those steps can work together. A short-lived environment gives a chance somewhere to run its tests. Staging provides another opportunity to validate it. A progressive rollout can expose a change to a small share of users, giving teams a chance to catch trouble and revert before it spreads. Policies can spell out which checks and approvals a production service requires, so developers have a repeatable path to release even as the volume of changes rises.

There’s a parallel in how Garfield thinks about GitOps. When he helped write its principles, the group specified versioned, immutable storage. That leaves room to explore how OCI or a versioned database might handle heavier concurrent use while preserving an auditable history.

“There are things that we’re going to have to continue to evolve to handle the scale and change rate,” Garfield said.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear Garfield explain how Argo maintainers use AI to triage and review pull requests, why he still wants predictable builds, and how one person used Google Sheets to do GitOps. They called it “SheetOps.”

item.title: Confluent spent 3 months rewriting Kafka’s Java client in Rust with AI — and had to start over
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Confluent spent nearly three months using AI coding agents to translate Apache Kafka’s Java client into Rust. The engineers discarded

The post Confluent spent 3 months rewriting Kafka’s Java client in Rust with AI — and had to start over appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Confluent spent nearly three months using AI coding agents to translate Apache Kafka’s Java client into Rust. The engineers discarded their first implementation, uncovered performance problems that slipped past automated tests, and eventually settled on a multi-agent workflow they believe could keep non-Java clients in step with Kafka as it evolves.

The work, detailed Tuesday in a technical blog post by Confluent principal engineer and Apache Kafka committer Andrew Schofield, began with Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 and progressed through several model upgrades. Confluent has since released its first generally available Rust client translated from Apache Kafka 4.4.0 alongside a preview of a new Python client.

The engineers applied 191 upstream Kafka commits representing several months of development to the translated codebase in less than two working days.

The engineers applied 191 upstream Kafka commits representing several months of development to the translated codebase in less than two working days. Confluent plans to build a continuous translation pipeline to keep its non-Java clients aligned with future Kafka releases.

Kafka’s Java client problem

Apache Kafka provides only a Java client, yet Confluent Cloud handles nearly as many connections from non-Java clients. Confluent’s existing non-Java clients rely on librdkafka, whose threading and memory management differ from the Java implementation.

With more than 100 active Kafka contributors and typically more than 20 Kafka Improvement Proposals per release, Confluent wants to derive its non-Java clients directly from the Java source through AI-assisted translation and maintain feature parity through a shared Rust core.

Three agents, one translation

Two engineers each devoted about 75% of their time to the experiment. Within two weeks, they had a working Rust producer without secure connections. TLS and authentication followed by week four, and a basic consumer was running by week six.

After several weeks, the team scrapped its original translation and started over with more specific instructions.

The agents frequently turned to engineers for guidance on Kafka’s architecture. After several weeks, the team scrapped its original translation and started over with more specific instructions.

Under Confluent’s translation workflow, a Project Manager agent coordinates the Actor and Critic. Engineers approve both milestone and phase plans and weigh in on architectural decisions, such as mapping Java threads to Tokio tasks.

The Actor and Critic communicate through Git. The Actor commits translated code and addresses the Critic’s findings until no further issues are raised. Schofield says the review cycle typically takes about five iterations.

When tests pass anyway

Although the generated code passed the translated Kafka tests, performance testing revealed a sleep operation on every iteration of the networking loop.

Confluent subsequently refined its translation instructions to specify the intended behavior rather than rely solely on the original source code and translated tests. Passing tests alone was insufficient to verify the quality of agent-generated code.

While the agents translated the code, engineers worked with Rust experts to design interfaces that preserved Kafka compatibility without imposing Java conventions on Rust developers. The team went through six candidate designs to ensure the Rust core could handle timeouts without interfering with signal handling in other language runtimes.

Toward continuous Kafka translation

When Apache Kafka 4.4.0 came out, the team opted to bring its existing Rust implementation up to date instead of starting from scratch. It took less than two working days to incorporate 191 upstream commits.

Confluent has yet to show whether it can keep multiple client implementations in sync as Kafka evolves or how much work engineers will need to do along the way. Schofield expects the continuous translation pipeline to begin doing that work in mid-2027.

The source code is available under the Apache License 2.0. While Confluent joins a broader wave of agent-driven Rust rewrites, its goal is to maintain the translated code over successive Kafka releases.

“Getting code quickly was only the beginning; making it useful across languages was the real engineering work.”

“Getting code quickly was only the beginning; making it useful across languages was the real engineering work,” Schofield wrote.
